items.body:
In her speech to the CBI, Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, delivered one of the most detailed explanations we have had from a minister as to what Andy Burnham means when he calls for more public control of utilities.

She said that the government was not against markets, and that in areas like telecoms privatisation had worked. But in water and energy it hadn’t, she insisted. She suggested that, in wanting more public control in these sectors, the government was aligned with the US, “hardly a hotbed of state socialism”.

She said:

Now I know the word privatisation can start an argument. So let me be precise. This is not about whether markets work. They do. Where there is genuine competition, as in telecoms, markets have given consumers choice and kept prices low while delivering infrastructure.
The social licence to operate must be won every day by building trust and having the best value, product or service. Where competition exists, it should be left to thrive, supported by our strong, independent Competition and Markets Authority.
But when it comes to essential services, we have spent four decades trying and failing to recreate market conditions when consumers have no alternative.
Public control is about getting the right outcomes. It’s not ideological. Ownership is not a requirement. We took the railway back into public ownership because it wasn’t working for passengers or the taxpayer. But we want Great British Railways to be challenged by open access operators in Greater Manchester’s Bee Network, which you may have heard of. Routes are set by the elected mayor to benefit the community. The services are still run by private operators.
Delivering the homes we need depends on a buoyant developer sector.
Looking at water and energy, we must accept that the status quo is not the neutral, pragmatic, centre ground. It’s the outlier, an exception that no other nation is trying to emulate.
Around the world, the core infrastructure of water overwhelmingly stays in public hands. England is almost unique in handing the entire system to private owners. The only other country in that corner with us is Chile.
We are also one of the few countries in Europe whose electricity and gas transmission networks are entirely privately owned. And here’s the irony. Foreign governments now own a bigger share of our utilities than the British government does – significant stakes in our water, electricity and gas networks, returns paid to their taxpayers.
I welcome that investment. Let me be clear about that. But it raises a question: why do other governments see the strategic and commercial value in holding Britain’s essential assets, when for 40 years the British government couldn’t?
And it isn’t just Europe. Look at the United States of America, hardly a hotbed of state socialism. Most Americans get their water from a public utility. Fewer than one in 10 get it from a private one. Community-owned power companies serve one in seven American electricity customers in Los Angeles and Seattle, in Nashville, in Austin, and the federal government still owns the Tennessee Valley Authority, one of the biggest power companies in the country. Nobody thinks America is anti-business.
So let’s be honest with ourselves. The status quo is the ideological position, and saying so should not be taboo.

Haigh also said that past governments had resorted to trying to make the privatisation of utilities work through excessive regulation.

To make the experiment work, successive governments leant on regulation, first to try to recreate competition from monopolies through a spreadsheet; then to manage what private markets would never price on their own, like the spare capacity that keeps the lights on; then to deliver social policy, treated as a free good because it went on the bill, not the budget.
Ofgem now has six times the staff it had in the early 2000s, almost three times the administrative budget in real terms, and a rule book more than six times longer. We’ve got a hulking, complex behemoth of a regulatory state. It satisfies no one. Not consumers, not investors. When you prioritise everything, you prioritise nothing.
In the fog of complexity, bad actors can thrive, while the rest of us can’t move with a clarity and pace this moment demands.
That is why public control should not alarm anyone in this room. It’s not ideological. It’s pragmatic, and it’s essential – for people, for places, and for business.
We will measure our progress against three tests: affordability, investability, accountability.

items.title: Mexican soldiers attacked in wake of drug lord's arrest
items.summary: Eight suspects are arrested after firing on soldiers trying to re-establish order following the arrest of 'El Chapo Isidro'.
items.body:
Image source, Daniel Cardenas/Anadolu via Getty Images

Image caption,

Extra forces have been deployed to guard the facility where 'Chapo Isidro' is in custody

ByVanessa Buschschlüter

Latin America online editor

Mexican soldiers have detained eight alleged members of a drug cartel whose leader was arrested on Friday, sparking a wave of violence in northern Sinaloa state.

The Mexican defence ministry said the soldiers were shot by the suspects on Sunday while on patrol in the town of Sinaloa de Leyva, trying to re-establish order in the wake of the arrest of Fausto Isidro Meza Flores.

Meza Flores, also known as "Chapo Isidro", was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list and had managed to evade capture for years.

The ministry said the eight had also been involved in the retaliatory violence unleashed by Meza Flores's cartel in the hours after his arrest on Friday.

In a statement published on social media, external, the ministry of defence said that one of the detainees was under age.

It added that its special forces had seized six vehicles as part of their operation, two of which had been fitted with bullet-proof armour and gun turrets.

The US Department of Justice described Friday's arrest of Meza Flores as "a spectacular military operation" and congratulated Mexico's military and special forces on his capture.

It said that the US Homeland Security Task Force had supported the Mexican military and praised the "bilateral effort".

Figure caption,

Watch: Suspected drug lord 'El Chapo Isidro' transferred to Mexico's capital

Mexico's defence ministry said its special forces had used stealth and surprise to reach the home of the wanted man.

They also established a security perimeter to prevent Meza Flores from escaping and cartel reinforcements from arriving.

Nevertheless, a bloody firefight ensued.

Along with Meza Flores, his second-in-command, known as "Serafín", and his financial operator, were also arrested and quickly transferred by air to Mexico City.

As news of their arrest spread, members of their cartel erected barricades on major roads and set cars and some shops alight.

There were also reports of shoot-outs between the security forces and cartel members.

The prosecutor's office in Sinaloa says 17 people, four of them members of the Mexican security forces, were killed as a result of the violence on Friday and early Saturday.

Who is 'Chapo Isidro'?

US Assistant Attorney General A Tysen Duva has described Meza Flores as "the most dangerous man in Mexico".

"For decades Meza Flores has promoted the terrorist objectives of the Sinaloa cartel," Duva said, accusing him of "flooding the United States with deadly substances".

The 44-year-old is believed to have started his criminal career with the Juárez cartel decades ago.

He later moved on to become the right-hand man of the leader of the Beltrán Leyva Organisation, a drug gang once allied to the Sinaloa cartel before the two groups split and became bitter enemies.

As early as 2013, the US Treasury identified Meza Flores as the leader of his own drug-trafficking organisation, named after him.

The US Treasury said at the time, that the Meza Flores drug trafficking organisation was responsible for "the distribution of large quantities of methamphetamine, heroin, marijuana, and cocaine to the United States".

It added that the turf war between the Meza Flores cartel and the Sinaloa cartel had "resulted in the quadrupling of drug-war killings" in between 2009 and 2013.

According to think tank Insight Crime, external, Meza Flores himself kept a low profile over the last decade while continuing to run his cartel out of Guasave, in Sinaloa state.

The head of the US Drug Enforcement Administration said that his capture was a "significant blow to a ruthless criminal organisation that has used extreme violence to traffic deadly drugs, including fentanyl, a designated weapon of mass destruction, into American communities".

His arrest, and the co-operation between US and Mexican officials which led to it, will be seen as a win for the government of Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum.

Sheinbaum has stressed that she is keen to work with the US authorities to capture high-profile target as long as Mexican's sovereignty is respected.

At least, everybody needs to have the credible path to get there.” “These investments are also a boon to prosperity. There are dividends to be gained from investing more in defence. The high street retailer said its own systems had not been compromised by the hack. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images

The high street retailer said its own systems had not been compromised by the hack. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images

Next issues cyber-attack warning after ‘benign’ data accessed by hackers

Retailer says it believes no personal data that could lead to fraud was accessed after hack of third-party supplier

• Business live – latest updates

Next has warned that hackers have gained access to data relating to the clothing and homewares retailer through a technology supplier.

The firm said on Monday that it had been informed that one of its third-party suppliers had “experienced a cyber incident” resulting in unauthorised access to the data.

The high street chain said it believed that customers’ personal data had not been compromised and the information affected was “limited in nature and, based on our current assessment, cannot be used to facilitate fraud against our customers or Next”.

It is understood the data accessed does not include information such as contact details, addresses, passwords or bank details, which could be used to commit fraud.

It said Next’s systems had not been compromised, though it was “affecting the supplier’s environment” in its business.

Investigations into the hack are in progress. Next said in a statement to investors: “Despite the limited and benign nature of the affected data, we are treating the matter with the utmost seriousness and are working closely with the supplier, law enforcement and relevant regulatory authorities.”

The latest incident comes amid a spate of cyber-attacks against high-profile retailers around the world.

Last week it emerged that a secret UK government cybersecurity operation had warded off the risk of a cyber-attack on fridges and freezers in UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums.

That came after hackers caused many millions of euros of damage in continental Europe, with attacks on fridge and freezer control systems in recent months.

Fashion retailers including the owner of Hobbs and Whistles, TFG London, and the online fashion seller Asos have faced cyber-attacks in which customer data was accessed.

Last year, several other British retailers, including Marks & Spencer, the Co-op and Harrods, were hit by damaging cyber incidents which affected operations for months.

items.body: US president praises Nvidia’s reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO, calling it ‘the correct and proper decision’ Sign up to the Breaking News US email Nvidia ’s shares have surged by 31% at the start of trading following the news. The S+P 500 jumped 4.5% and is recovering nearly half of its brutal losses from last week, which was one of its worst since the 2008 financial crisis. Rallies for AI stocks had the Nasdaq composite up a market-leading 6.5%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 1,117 points. Here’s Trump ’s full social media post, in which he also called Jensen Huang “a Great Patriot and National Treasure”. The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO. The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy. The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct. On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure. Separately, NVIDIA should continue its thorough internal investigation of the Company’s compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and Patriotic Duty to protect U.S. National Security. Congratulations to Jensen, the NVIDIA Board, to the People of the United States — and, indeed, the World! Continue reading...

items.summary: Authorities say they believe the Saturday night shooting at a concert in Strathmore ‘may be gang-related’ Nine people were shot at a concert in central California , leaving one person critically injured with a chest injury, the local sheriff said Sunday. The shooting broke out at about 7.30pm Saturd…
items.body:
The shooting broke out Saturday night at a concert attended by about 150 people in Strathmore, authorities said. Photograph: Matt Rourke/AP

The shooting broke out Saturday night at a concert attended by about 150 people in Strathmore, authorities said. Photograph: Matt Rourke/AP

Nine people shot at central California concert with one in critical condition

Authorities say they believe the Saturday night shooting at a concert in Strathmore ‘may be gang-related’

Nine people were shot at a concert in central California, leaving one person critically injured with a chest injury, the local sheriff said Sunday.

The shooting broke out at about 7.30pm Saturday at a concert attended by about 150 people in Strathmore, a small town in Tulare county, a mountainous region in the center of the state, the local sheriff’s department said in a statement. An unspecified number of suspects opened fire on the crowd. No arrests were announced.

One 26-year-old man was shot in the chest and required surgery. He remained in critical condition, the sheriff’s department said. Two other victims ages 19 and 22 also required surgery, while six people sustained minor injuries.

Authorities said that they believe the shooting “may be gang-related” but didn’t elaborate. The show in the town of roughly 3,000 people featured performers from neighboring states, the department said.

The department didn’t immediately respond to emailed questions seeking further details but said there was no longer any immediate threat to the public.

As of Monday, there had been more than 420 mass shootings in the US so far for the year, according to the Gun Violence Archive. The archive, a nonpartisan resources, defines mass shootings as cases in which four or more victims are either wounded or killed.

High numbers of mass shootings reported annually in the US have prompted many to call for more substantial federal gun control. But Congress over the years has not passed such restrictions.

items.title: Amtrak train derails after colliding with tractor-trailer in Louisiana
items.summary: Five passengers were reported to have non-life-threatening injuries after crash at railroad crossing near Lafayette An Amtrak train collided with a tractor-trailer at a railroad crossing in south-central Louisiana , derailing the lead locomotive and two baggage cars while injuring some passengers on…
items.body:
A derailed Amtrak train in Louisiana on 22 November 2026. Photograph: Lafayette police department

A derailed Amtrak train in Louisiana on 22 November 2026. Photograph: Lafayette police department

Amtrak train derails after colliding with tractor-trailer in Louisiana

Five passengers were reported to have non-life-threatening injuries after crash at railroad crossing near Lafayette

An Amtrak train collided with a tractor-trailer at a railroad crossing in south-central Louisiana, derailing the lead locomotive and two baggage cars while injuring some passengers on Sunday evening, officials said.

Five passengers who were reported hurt were said to have injuries that were not life-threatening.

The train in question was the Sunset Limited, traveling from California to New Orleans. It collided with the 18-wheeler, which was carrying a bulldozer, near Lafayette, Louisiana – about 135 miles (217km) west of New Orleans – at about 6.15pm local time.

“All passenger cars remained upright,” and 95 customers were on board, Amtrak said in a statement reported by ABC News.

Sgt Ashley Wood of the Lafayette police department said reported injuries were minor and that a few passengers had been transported to a hospital.

The Lafayette fire department later released an update saying at least five of the passengers had been injured.

“Hazmat and Rescue personnel ensured the scene was safe for first responders to assist the injured and check on the other passengers,” Lafayette fire officials also said in a statement, according to ABC News.

“Once it was safe for passengers to exit, firefighters assisted them to a safe location along with their luggage.”

Monique Blanco Boulet, Lafayette’s mayor, reiterated in a statement on social media that the Sunset Limited’s passengers were being transported to New Orleans by bus.

A passenger who spoke with the Acadian Advocate newspaper said she “felt two jolts”.

“The first one was light but noticeable. The second one was so forceful it just knocked over everything we had on our table – water, books, everything,” said the passenger, who was identified by the outlet only as Nicole.

Two New York natives, identified only as Ralph and Eli, said “things were going great” because the Giants football team that they support was on its way to winning a game at the time. “Then suddenly we felt a massive jolt, and the train started decelerating very fast,” Ralph said, according to the Advocate.

The newspaper reported that an investigation indicated that the tractor-trailer was trying to cross the tracks and got stuck. After the semi got stuck, the crossing arm came down because of the approaching train.

The train slowed down but was not able to stop, Lafayette news station KATC reported.

Various estimates show there are roughly three train derailments daily in the US, involving various kinds of trains and for various reasons – with most of those cases not leading to major disaster.

A derailed Amtrak train in Louisiana on 22 November 2026. Photograph: Lafayette police department
Amtrak train derails after colliding with tractor-trailer in Louisiana
Five passengers were reported to have non-life-threatening injuries after crash at railroad crossing near Lafayette

An Amtrak train collided with a tractor-trailer at a railroad crossing in south-central Louisiana, derailing the lead locomotive and two baggage cars while injuring some passengers on Sunday evening, officials said.
Five passengers who were reported hurt were said to have injuries that were not life-threatening.

The train in question was the Sunset Limited, traveling from California to New Orleans. It collided with the 18-wheeler, which was carrying a bulldozer, near Lafayette, Louisiana – about 135 miles (217km) west of New Orleans – at about 6.15pm local time.
“All passenger cars remained upright,” and 95 customers were on board, Amtrak said in a statement reported by ABC News.
Sgt Ashley Wood of the Lafayette police department said reported injuries were minor and that a few passengers had been transported to a hospital.
The Lafayette fire department later released an update saying at least five of the passengers had been injured.

“Hazmat and Rescue personnel ensured the scene was safe for first responders to assist the injured and check on the other passengers,” Lafayette fire officials also said in a statement, according to ABC News.
“Once it was safe for passengers to exit, firefighters assisted them to a safe location along with their luggage.”
Monique Blanco Boulet, Lafayette’s mayor, reiterated in a statement on social media that the Sunset Limited’s passengers were being transported to New Orleans by bus.
A passenger who spoke with the Acadian Advocate newspaper said she “felt two jolts”.

“The first one was light but noticeable. The second one was so forceful it just knocked over everything we had on our table – water, books, everything,” said the passenger, who was identified by the outlet only as Nicole.

Two New York natives, identified only as Ralph and Eli, said “things were going great” because the Giants football team that they support was on its way to winning a game at the time. “Then suddenly we felt a massive jolt, and the train started decelerating very fast,” Ralph said, according to the Advocate.

The newspaper reported that an investigation indicated that the tractor-trailer was trying to cross the tracks and got stuck. After the semi got stuck, the crossing arm came down because of the approaching train.
The train slowed down but was not able to stop, Lafayette news station KATC reported.
Various estimates show there are roughly three train derailments daily in the US, involving various kinds of trains and for various reasons – with most of those cases not leading to major disaster.

items.title: Presidential villa suffers water and power cuts, Nigerian leader says
items.summary: Bola Tinubu says he was shaving last week when the water cut out - an experience familiar to many Nigerians.
items.body:
Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

Tinubu made the disclosure at a special prayer session organised in his honour by members of his family

ByMansur Abubakar

Reporting fromAbuja

Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu says the presidential villa suffers from cuts in electricity and water - failures that plague ordinary citizens.

He said he was shaving last week when the water supply at the villa, known as Aso Rock, in Abuja cut.

He is seeking re-election next January and vowed to address these issues..

Tinubu made the disclosure on Sunday at a special prayer session organised in his honour by members of his family in Lagos.

He explained: "On the Wednesday of last week, I was shaving, and the water went off. In the villa, you won't know punishment dey dia too [there’s punishment there too in Nigerian pidgin].

"The water went off. So we will correct all this. No light, no water, no electricity, no development. We have just started. We can do it, and we will do it for Nigeria,” he said.

Aso Villa serves as both the office and official residence of the Nigerian president. It is situated at the base of Aso Rock in Abuja.

Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

Many Nigerians rely on generators like these to power their homes and businesses

Nigeria has long endured electricity shortages, but recent severe disruptions have been caused primarily by insufficient gas supplies and declining hydropower output, rather than the usual nationwide grid collapse.

Persistent blackouts in Lagos, Abuja and elsewhere have forced distribution companies to implement rotating power cuts, severely impacting households and businesses.

The country also suffers from chronic water shortages, the result of a structural crisis rooted in the gap between rapid urban population growth and decaying, inadequate public water infrastructure.

Tinubu made a high-profile electricity promise during the 2023 election campaign, but the exact wording and how binding it is has become a major point of contention ahead of the 16 January election.

Tinubu defeated the country’s former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar as well as Peter Obi in 2023 and the three are seen as the strongest contenders once again.

items.summary: Jurors hear Anthony Russell killed Soham murderer by hitting him repeatedly over head with metal bar A prisoner killed the Soham murderer Ian Huntley with a heavy metal bar in a “cold-blooded” attack that had been planned weeks in advance, a court heard. Jurors were told that Anthony Russell, 44, re…
items.body:
The prosecutor said jurors may feel ‘no sympathy’ for Huntley, pictured in August 2002, but they must base their verdict on the evidence. Photograph: PA

The prosecutor said jurors may feel ‘no sympathy’ for Huntley, pictured in August 2002, but they must base their verdict on the evidence. Photograph: PA

Ian Huntley killed by inmate in ‘cold-blooded murder’ planned weeks in advance, court told

Jurors hear Anthony Russell killed Soham murderer by hitting him repeatedly over head with metal bar

A prisoner killed the Soham murderer Ian Huntley with a heavy metal bar in a “cold-blooded” attack that had been planned weeks in advance, a court heard.

Jurors were told that Anthony Russell, 44, repeatedly hit the 52-year-old over the head in the attack at the high-security HMP Frankland, near Durham.

Matthew Bean KC, prosecuting, told jurors at Newcastle crown court that they may feel no sympathy for the Soham killer, who murdered Holly Wells and Jessica Chapman in 2002, but the case was not about his “appalling actions” but the manner in which he had died.

Russell denies a single count of murder.

Bean said: “At shortly after 9am on 26 February 2026, the prosecution say that the defendant in this trial, Anthony Russell, murdered Ian Huntley, by striking him repeatedly to the head with a heavy metal bar. The prosecution case is that this was a cold-blooded murder that had been planned weeks in advance of its execution.

“It happened in a prison, HMP Frankland, where both Anthony Russell and Ian Huntley were serving prisoners. At the time, both men were serving sentences of life imprisonment for offences of murder.

“The defendant, Anthony Russell, you will hear, had previously been convicted of the murder of three people, these offences having taken place in October 2020. The name of the man he killed, Ian Huntley, will be known to many, if not all of you.

“He had been convicted of the murder of two girls, Holly Wells and Jessica Chapman, that took place in the village of Soham in Cambridgeshire in August 2002. These were offences that, for entirely understandable reasons, aroused feelings of disgust and anger.

“Due to the nature of his offences, you may feel little or no sympathy for what happened to him. More than that, the prosecution do not ask for sympathy.

“Ultimately, this case is not about the appalling actions of Ian Huntley during his life, but the manner of his death. The prosecution well understands the emotions that may be stirred during this trial.

“It is essential, however, to be true to your oath or affirmation, to put emotion to one side, to try this case on the evidence and the evidence alone, and to come to verdicts based on that evidence.”

Bean told jurors the two murderers were held on A wing at the high-security prison and there had been “tension” between them in the months leading up to the killing.

About a year earlier, in March 2025, prison staff witnessed an argument between them in which they threatened one another and had to be separated.

They later agreed with staff that nothing further would happen, the court heard.

About 10 months later, Russell was seen with a black eye, and told staff he had fallen.

Bean said: “Some members of staff believed, however, that someone had assaulted him and you will hear some evidence during the trial that indicates that it may have been caused by Ian Huntley.”

Those incidents were the only two issues between the men in the prison records, the court heard.

The trial continues.

The move – if…
items.body:
The SpaceX Starlink satellite network has been used by Ukrainian troops and could be at risk from Russian weapons in space. Photograph: SPACEX/AFP/Getty Images

The SpaceX Starlink satellite network has been used by Ukrainian troops and could be at risk from Russian weapons in space. Photograph: SPACEX/AFP/Getty Images

Germany taking seriously reports Russia may be planning to launch nuclear weapons into space

Move would breach nuclear weapons treaties and reports come amid rising concerns over militarisation of space

The German government has said it is taking very seriously reports that Russia may be planning to launch a satellite armed with a ⁠nuclear weapon ⁠into ​space later this year.

The move – if confirmed – would be a breach of 1967 Outer Space treaty of which Moscow is a signatory as well the 1963 Partial Nuclear Test Ban treaty – which prohibit the placing of nuclear weapons in Earth’s orbit and test detonations in space.

The reports by a group of German media outlets, based on what they said were assessments by western intelligence agencies, come amid a recent rise in concern over the increasing militarisation of space which had the US Air Force secretary, Troy Meink, admit for the first time in September that Washington had deployed “on-orbit space control weapons”.

Germany’s Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND) intelligence service and armed forces have exchanged ⁠intelligence showing that a Russian satellite, named Sputnik-S, ​was assembled several ‌years ago ‌and is stationed in the Moscow region, ‌a report by broadcasters NDR and WDR, and newspaper Sueddeutsche Zeitung said.

According to the reports, warnings in early November said the satellite could be launched within 60 days and would be operational shortly afterwards.

“No, we haven’t seen ‌the report. But there are so many ‘alleged’ ​and ‘possible’ claims in it, attributed to who knows whom, that ⁠it’s certainly hardly worth ​taking ​them seriously,” Kremlin spokesperson ​Dmitry Peskov told ​reporters.

The Russian embassy in Berlin said it was not aware of any such plans describing the reports as “unfounded allegations regarding the space activities of the Russian Federation” and calling them “part of a propaganda campaign”.

Moscow’s space measures, the embassy added, proceed “in accordance with international obligations” and serve “exclusively peaceful purposes”.

In 2024, Russia denied assertions by ​US officials that Moscow was developing a weapon that could destroy enemy satellites by setting off a nuclear explosion in ⁠space and triggering an electromagnetic pulse (EMP) to disable the electronic systems of nearby satellites.

US officials have alleged that Russia ​has ​for years been developing ​a nuclear weapon capable of ​destroying ‌entire satellite networks, ​such ​as SpaceX’s vast Starlink internet system that Ukrainian troops have been using.

Concern has been mounting in recent years in Europe and the US that Russia has been seeking to develop an anti-satellite weapon system which experts believe would probably employ an EMP wave.

Two years ago, the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, denied the claim after then US president Joe Biden’s national security spokesperson John Kirby confirmed that the Russian Federation had been developing a “troubling” anti-satellite weapon.

“We’re not talking about a weapon that can be used to attack human beings or cause physical destruction here on Earth,” Kirby said.

Biden told reporters in 2024 that he believed Russia was developing the “capacity to launch a system into space that could theoretically do something that was damaging … my hope is it will not”.

While EMPs can occur naturally, it has long been understood that nuclear detonation has the ability to harm electronic systems, including energy networks, with both the US and Russia conducting high altitude tests in the early 1960s.

There has been increasing discussion over fears that Russia may be planning to place a nuclear weapon in space. Germany’s top military space commander earlier this year said he could not rule out that Russia was working on technology to place a nuclear warhead in space, warning that such a move could cripple satellite services and make parts of the orbit unusable for decades.

“At the very top end of escalation, there is the suspicion that Russia may be working on technology to place a nuclear explosive device in orbit,” Maj Gen Michael Traut, commander of the German Space Command, said in an interview with Politico.

Asked whether he considered that realistic, Traut said: “I cannot rule it out.” He added that a nuclear detonation in space could impact up to a third of satellites in low Earth orbit with massive global consequences.

Suspicions over Russia’s ambitions to place weapons in space were given fresh scrutiny in 2022 with the launch of the Kosmos 2553 test satellite, which US and intelligence sources suggested could be a dummy run for the deployment of a nuclear weapon in space.

items.summary: Chipmaker reverses decision it made to remove chief executive after reports of affairs including with alleged Chinese spy Business live – latest updates Nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive in a stunning reversal following his dramatic resignation after reports of extramarital affai…
items.body:
Jensen Huang built Nvidia from a video-game chip designer into the dominant supplier of AI processors. Photograph: Hannibal Hanschke/EPA

Jensen Huang built Nvidia from a video-game chip designer into the dominant supplier of AI processors. Photograph: Hannibal Hanschke/EPA

Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO

Chipmaker reverses decision it made to remove chief executive after reports of affairs including with alleged Chinese spy

• Business live – latest updates

Nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive in a stunning reversal after his dramatic resignation after reports of extramarital affairs including with an alleged Chinese spy.

Nvidia shares surged on the news, jumping more than 25% as stock markets opened in New York on Monday, while Donald Trump, who had called for Huang’s return, said “the country needs Jensen’s leadership”.

The chipmaker’s move to bring Huang back marks a sharp reversal from its board’s decision days earlier to rule out his return. Trump said the US government had no “evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct”.

Nvidia stock surges after Jensen Huang rehired as CEO – business live

Read more

In a statement, the company said its board directors had talked to Huang and were “satisfied with respect to Mr Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia”. Nvidia added that it had received input from “senior levels” of the US government and was confident his reinstatement “poses no national security risk”.

Nvidia said an independent investigation into allegations that Huang was the target of a Chinese intelligence operation, which included having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, is still ongoing and “will proceed to conclusion.”

Harvey Jones, the Nvidia chair, who was appointed this month after Huang’s resignation on 12 November, said: “The board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers.”

Huang built Nvidia from a video-game chip designer into the dominant supplier of AI processors, steering its roadmap, customer deals and Washington ties along the way.

He resigned after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with a businesswoman whom US authorities suspect of spying for China, an allegation Beijing denies.

Trump had called for Huang’s reinstatement overnight, posting on Truth Social: “I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang. It would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A. President DONALD J. TRUMP.”

Trump said the US government had no reason to believe Huang’s return posed a risk to national security, adding that the attorney general, Todd Blanche, had “confirmed that the US government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct”.

He praised Nvidia’s board for making “the correct and proper decision” and said: “The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy.”

It came hours after reports that Alice Huang, the Chinese businesswoman at the heart of the scandal, had been in contact with an official in China’s spy agency while she was having an affair with Huang. People with knowledge of US intelligence reports claimed she was in touch with the Chinese official until this autumn, according to the New York Times.

skip past newsletter promotion

after newsletter promotion

Trading on the prediction website Polymarket on Sunday indicated a sharply rising expectation that Huang would be restored. The probability among the site’s users rose from about 10% to 18% overnight as Huang overtook Ian Buck, another senior Nvidia executive, in the market for the next CEO of Nvidia. Tens of millions of dollars were wagered on that and similar predictions.

The Arm Holdings chief executive, Rene Haas, who had been approached to succeed Huang, has signed a new deal that will keep him in his current role until 2033.

Elon Musk, who had called for Huang to return, posted on X: “Welcome back the main man,” alongside a picture of him shaking hands with Huang.

Dan Ives, a senior tech analyst, said the Nvidia board had to perform an about-turn because the alternative – a core company in the AI boom entering a crucial period without its CEO and founder – was “the bigger risk to shareholders”.

“At the end of the day despite this Jensen saga the board knew it had no choice but to bring him back and for the US technology sector this was the move it had to make,” Ives wrote in a note to shareholders,” he said.

Sam North, a market analyst at the trading platform etoro, said: “Jensen Huang’s return underlines how much of the AI trade still rests on one man.”

Almost one third of global greenhouse gas emissions are connected to the global food system through land clearing, raising animals, growing crops, processing, packaging, transport and waste. Photograph: Ekaterina Goncharova/Getty Images

Plant-based lunches could cut Australia’s emissions by 15m tonnes, new research shows

Nationwide change in lunch habits could cut more climate pollution than grounding every domestic flight

• Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Australians could collectively cut climate pollution by more than 15m tonnes – more than grounding every domestic flight – simply by changing what they eat for lunch.

A nationwide shift to plant-based lunches could reduce food-related emissions by 29% – 15.4m tonnes per year – while saving the average household about $611 annually, according to a report by Bryant Research and not-for-profit ProVeg.

Nadia Schilling, the executive director of ProVeg Australia, said the findings highlighted the “huge difference” that relatively modest changes, like a meat-free Monday or a plant-based lunch, could make.

That might mean opting for a black bean burrito, a poke bowl with tofu, or a lunchbox with hummus and fresh vegetables – instead of a cheese and ham wrap – she said.

“We realise that Australians aren’t going to change their diets overnight,” Schilling said. “This is a really practical change where everyone wins. Lunch is a huge missed opportunity.”

The root-to-tip revolution! An A-Z of how to eat plants in full – for extra flavour, fibre and savings

Read more

Australia has the highest per capita food-related emissions in the world, the report found. It modelled the environmental, health and economic impacts for a range of Australia-wide dietary changes, finding the shift to 100% plant-based meals would cut dietary emissions by two-thirds, while just switching lunches would cut nearly one-third.

Emissions from domestic aviation are about 10m tonnes a year, according to government data.

The organisations behind the report, which promote moving from meat to plant-rich foods and alternative protein sources, called for a national campaign to increase vegetable consumption along with policy and funding support for plant proteins.

Almost one-third of global greenhouse gas emissions are connected to the global food system through land clearing, raising animals, growing crops, processing, packaging, transport and waste.

Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email

The National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) is reviewing the evidence about sustainability and diet as part of the first update of Australian dietary guidelines in more than 13 years. Draft guidelines are expected to be released for public consultation in December 2026.

An NHMRC spokesperson said the expert committee drafting the new guidelines had prioritised information on health impacts, but “information about the economic, social, and environmental sustainability of diets was then considered as one of the many factors that influence people’s ability to follow a healthy diet”.

Dr Diana Bogueva, who researches food sustainability at Curtin University, said relatively small changes in everyday eating habits – when adopted by a large number of people – could have a major impact on the environmental footprint of food production.

skip past newsletter promotion

after newsletter promotion

However, Bogueva, who was not involved with the report, said the environmental, health and affordability benefits of eating less meat depended on what foods replaced it.

Whole foods like legumes, grains, vegetables, nuts and seeds provided valuable fibre, vitamins, minerals and plant proteins, she said. “But not every plant-based product is automatically healthy,” Bogueva said. “Simply swapping meat for highly processed products does not necessarily improve the nutritional quality of the meal.”

Sustainable eating didn’t have to be expensive, she added, and some of the most nutritious sources of plant protein – such as beans, lentils and chickpeas – were also among the most affordable.

“We do know there are both health and environmental benefits if you reduce red and processed meat in your diet,” said Alexandra Jones, an associate professor at the George Institute for Global Health, who was not involved with the report.

But rather than focusing on swapping out one protein for another, the emphasis should be on “helping people eat more vegetables, legumes and minimally processed plant foods,” she said.

A good lunch could be as simple as an “old-school salad sandwich” on wholegrain bread, with lettuce, tomato, sprouts and beetroot.

items.body:
Carmakers are being urged to adopt safety principles to help stop the misuse of smart car functions by perpetrators of domestic violence. Photograph: d3sign/Getty Images

Carmakers are being urged to adopt safety principles to help stop the misuse of smart car functions by perpetrators of domestic violence. Photograph: d3sign/Getty Images

Domestic violence perpetrators are misusing smart car features to abuse, researchers warn

Exclusive: Alarming report reveals how tracking and monitoring functions and digital key access have been used to facilitate abuse

• Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Earlier this year a man in Australia was found guilty of using a connected car app to harass his former partner, including restricting the speed at which she could drive, sometimes to 40km an hour.

In 2022 in the US, a woman found her former husband had used a car app associated with her car to track her; the carmaker then allegedly refused to terminate the former partner’s digital access to the vehicle.

In another case in the US in 2020, a woman found a baseball bat her former partner had used to threaten her in the back seat of her car.

How one woman’s Tesla was remotely controlled – and used to harass her – by an abusive ex-partner

Read more

These three cases form part of an alarming report by University of New South Wales researchers, released on Tuesday, which warned this was an emerging problem that could get worse. It found smart car functions that could be misused by perpetrators of domestic violence to facilitate abuse were prevalent across major car brands.

“There is an urgent need for carmakers to adopt safety by design principles from the early stages of designing both the apps and the cars,” said the report co-author Katharine Kemp, a data privacy and consumer protection expert at UNSW.

The researchers found that problems emerged as many of the cars’ functions – which include tracking and monitoring functions, remote control functions and digital key access – could be controlled remotely via an app.

The researchers said that there were three main scenarios that could open the functions to misuse: the abuser being the owner of the car and having created the account themselves; they were granted access as a secondary user of the car; or the victim survivor is impersonated and the perpetrator creates an account on their behalf.

Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email

The report said that the problematic functions are mainly marketed by the car manufacturers as being for the purpose of enabling the car owner to “keep an eye on” and protect their car.

It highlighted an advertisement on the carmaker Kia’s Australian website for “Kia Connect”. Kia was contacted for comment.

“Kia Connect is also bundled with geofence and time fencing alerts which let the owner know when another user strays outside preset limits of geographical areas or time limitations. It’s a perfect feature for anyone dealing with a family member who is borrowing the car,” the advertisement said.

The report mapped how prevalent potentially problematic functions were, and whether these functions were advertised by 15 of the top car brands.

One of the functions raised was geolocation, which allows the geographical location of the car in real-time or when it is parked, and was advertised by 100% of the 15 car brands, with some marketing it as “Vehicle Tracking”, “Vehicle Locator” or “Find My Car”. The researchers said this tool could be misused to track people.

The researchers found that 60% of the top 15 brands also advertised a “zone exit alert” which allows users to set an alarm if a car leaves a designated area. They warned this functions could be used to: “Set a zone of 3km from the family home to receive alert if the victim-survivor attempts to leave or fails to follow abuser’s rules limiting travel by the victim-survivor.”

Meanwhile, 20% advertise speed or acceleration restrictions. The explanation of this function by carmakers includes that it is to set speed limits for young drivers or valet parkers.

But the report warned this could be misused to set a speed limit of 40km/h so that a victim survivor cannot safely use highways or escape at speed.

The researchers also raised concerns about digital key access, which allows drivers to use their mobile phone to unlock the car or start the engine and was advertised by 67% of car brands in the Australian market. The report warns: “This function may also allow an abuser to remotely terminate or severely restrict the victim survivor’s ability to use the vehicle.

“An abuser can achieve this, for example, by remotely deactivating the victim-survivor’s digital key access or setting speed restrictions on the vehicle. This could effectively strand the victim-survivor in an unsafe location and/or limit the victim survivor’s ability to escape the abuser’s violence,” the report said.

skip past newsletter promotion

after newsletter promotion

‘Almost no accountability’ for manufacturers

Emma Buxton-Namisnyk, a co-author of the report, warned this was an emerging problem that could get worse.

“There’s really not a widespread understanding about how these technologies can be misused,” she said, adding that there was “almost no accountability” for car manufacturers to limit potential misuses.

The report recommended carmakers adopt principles which consider at the design phase how a function could be misused to facilitate abuse, and help determine if a function should not be offered because the risks outweigh the benefits.

Last year the eSafety commissioner, Julie Inman Grant, raised the alarm on the issue after receiving reports from frontline workers that cars were being used to monitor and track victim-survivors of domestic violence.

She called for improved industry safeguards, noting that it was estimated that more than 90% of new cars sold in Australia by 2031 would have embedded connectivity.

“We need urgent action to make them safer,” Inman Grant said.

The minister for social services, Tanya Plibersek, said in a statement to Guardian Australia that the government was considering what more it could do to crack down on the risk posed by smart devices, after developing a support service on technology-facilitated abuse that helps frontline workers navigate the issue.

“We’re seeing new frontiers of family and domestic violence emerge every day – we’ve seen smart fridges, cat feeders and electric vehicles all being weaponised to stalk, control and harm,” she said.

“We’ll consider what more we can do as we finalise our Second Action Plan to End Violence Against Women and Children.”

Smartglasses such as Meta’s Ray-Bans, which have…

Smartglasses such as Meta’s Ray-Bans, which can have built-in cameras, microphones and AI assistants, have been banned at some pools and playgrounds. Photograph: Carlos Barría/Reuters

‘Pervert glasses’ named word of the year by Macquarie dictionary, ahead of ‘nudify’ and ‘AI;DR’

Australian dictionary’s committee of word experts says winning term is ‘a succinct reflection of the state of the world in 2026’

• Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The backlash to “pervert glasses” has been swift and severe.

Smartglasses such as Meta’s Ray-Bans, which have built-in cameras, microphones, and AI assistants have been banned at some Australian swimming pools and playgrounds, and condemned as a possible invasion of privacy.

There are widespread fears about the glasses being used to film people, especially women, without their consent, and the resulting footage being posted on social media.

Now “pervert glasses” have gained a new layer of infamy: being crowned Macquarie dictionary’s word of the year.

The term “pervert glasses”, which also won the people’s choice word of the year for 2026, was described by the committee of word experts as a triumph of linguistics.

“The coinage pervert glasses is a succinct reflection of the state of the world in 2026 in so many ways,” they said.

Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email

“On the one hand, we’ve seen a massive acceleration in the capabilities of AI and products that integrate it. At the same time, the undeniably critical nickname mirrors the widespread calls to hit the brakes on this seemingly unchecked development.

‘Human’ wins Cambridge dictionary’s word of the year

Read more

“The name represents the year we’ve all endured, with AI, the manosphere, increasing surveillance in supermarkets, and more. Sure these new gadgets might be marketed as smart glasses or camera glasses, but it seems to us that pervert glasses paints a more apt reflection of the year.”

Honourable mentions from the committee went to “PMOS”, or polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, which has received greater recognition alongside spreading awareness of medical misogyny; “agentic”, which refers to the ability, especially of artificial intelligence, to make decisions independently; and “Marrickville pause”, a colloquial term referring to a temporary halt in conversation by people under Sydney’s flight path.

“Digital dementia”, which refers to short-term memory loss from a reliance on technology and artificial intelligence, received an honourable people’s choice mention.

The committee said digital dementia was “not a real medical diagnosis but that hasn’t stopped the fear of an increasing reliance on digital devices from resonating deeply”.

“People are finding that they’re struggling to navigate without Google Maps and to make and remember plans without iCal,” they said.

“It will be interesting to see if all of this outsourcing does in fact lead to impaired cognition in the long term.”

In a sign of the times, other words on the shortlist included “nudify”, referring to AI-generated pornography, and “AI;DR”, short for “AI; didn’t read”.

Last year, AI slop was dubbed the term that was the epitome of 2025 linguistics, with the committee saying it embodied the word of the year’s general theme of reflecting “a major aspect of society or societal change throughout the year”.

The committee’s choice and people’s choice winning words are chosen from the list of new entries included in the annual update of the Macquarie dictionary online. The people’s choice winner was selected from public votes cast on its website.

items.title: Flights and train services cancelled in Belgium due to strike
items.summary: A series of strikes have hit Belgium in recent months as the prime minister struggles to agree a budget to cut costs.
items.body:
Image source, Reuters

Image caption,

Brussels Airport is receiving no travellers until 21:00 on Monday

ByPaulin Kola

Hundreds of flights have been cancelled and train services have been severely disrupted across Belgium as a result of a strike against planned austerity measures.

All air traffic has been halted in Zaventem airport in the capital, Brussels, as well as Charlerois, home to low-cost airlines such as Ryanair.

Trains and underground services have also been halted in Brussels where large numbers of people are expected to join a protest march.

The protest comes as Prime Minister Bart De Wever has so far failed to agree a budget to cut costs with his coalition allies. King Philippe declined his resignation earlier this month, giving De Wever more time to negotiate.

No flights are taking off or landing at Brussels Airport between 07:00 and 21:00 local time (06:00-20:00 GMT) as a result of the strike by air traffic controllers. More than 50,000 travellers' plans were being disrupted - with more expected to be affected overnight and on Tuesday.

A similar situation has affected Charlerois, where all flights were shown as "scheduled", regardless of the time of departure of arrival.

"Without air traffic control, no flights can take off or land," the airport said on Saturday when the strike action was announced, warning of "disastrous consequences".

As thousands descended on Brussels for the protest march, the leader of one of the country's main unions, FGTB, said the government had alternatives to "dismantling the social protection system".

"A genuine wealth tax, fair taxation, and the elimination of tax loopholes," Bert Engelaar, head of FGBT, said.

"Political responsibility is not about keeping a government afloat at all costs. It's about knowing when to stop," Engelaar said, praising the left-wing Vooruit party - the only member of the five-party governing coalition reported to have stalled efforts to agree the budget.

Vooruit wants to raise taxes on the rich, and fewer cuts to pensions and the health sector.

Another union leader, Ann Vermorgen of the CSC, criticised government plans to cut bank holidays when they fall on weekends.

Public transport, schools and other public services are also facing disruptions.

Brussels Airport is receiving no travellers until 21:00 on Monday
ByPaulin Kola
Hundreds of flights have been cancelled and train services have been severely disrupted across Belgium as a result of a strike against planned austerity measures.
All air traffic has been halted in Zaventem airport in the capital, Brussels, as well as Charlerois, home to low-cost airlines such as Ryanair.
Trains and underground services have also been halted in Brussels where large numbers of people are expected to join a protest march.

The protest comes as Prime Minister Bart De Wever has so far failed to agree a budget to cut costs with his coalition allies. King Philippe declined his resignation earlier this month, giving De Wever more time to negotiate.

No flights are taking off or landing at Brussels Airport between 07:00 and 21:00 local time (06:00-20:00 GMT) as a result of the strike by air traffic controllers. More than 50,000 travellers' plans were being disrupted - with more expected to be affected overnight and on Tuesday.
A similar situation has affected Charlerois, where all flights were shown as "scheduled", regardless of the time of departure of arrival.
"Without air traffic control, no flights can take off or land," the airport said on Saturday when the strike action was announced, warning of "disastrous consequences".
As thousands descended on Brussels for the protest march, the leader of one of the country's main unions, FGTB, said the government had alternatives to "dismantling the social protection system".
"A genuine wealth tax, fair taxation, and the elimination of tax loopholes," Bert Engelaar, head of FGBT, said.

"Political responsibility is not about keeping a government afloat at all costs. It's about knowing when to stop," Engelaar said, praising the left-wing Vooruit party - the only member of the five-party governing coalition reported to have stalled efforts to agree the budget.
Vooruit wants to raise taxes on the rich, and fewer cuts to pensions and the health sector.
Another union leader, Ann Vermorgen of the CSC, criticised government plans to cut bank holidays when they fall on weekends.
Public transport, schools and other public services are also facing disruptions.

items.title: Environment Agency and Natural England face axe in Labour quango cull
items.summary: Louise Haigh says the two environmental regulators are being reviewed as part of shake-up of arm’s length bodies Ministers are considering abolishing two of England’s biggest environmental regulators in an attempt to give politicians greater control over what gets built and where. Louise Haigh, the…
items.body:
A badger sett in Hambledon, Surrey. Haigh did not push back against the idea Natural England was being targeted for abolition. Photograph: Lillian King/Getty Images

A badger sett in Hambledon, Surrey. Haigh did not push back against the idea Natural England was being targeted for abolition. Photograph: Lillian King/Getty Images

Natural England could be abolished as part of quango cull, says Louise Haigh

First secretary of state says proliferation of arms-length government bodies is hampering decision-making

The nature watchdog Natural England could be abolished as part of a cull of arm’s length government organisations, Louise Haigh has said.

Saying that the proliferation of quangos and other similar bodies had made decision-making by ministers more difficult, the first secretary of state said it could fall within a push to change the landscape of government by scrapping some organisations and bringing others into departments.

Abolishing Natural England could be justified on the basis that it could speed up planning decisions and thus boost housebuilding and growth, but removing or curbing its role would be likely to prompt concern from environmental groups.

Last month, the Conservatives announced that if they won power they would abolish both Natural England and the Environment Agency, saying this would help create more new homes.

Louise Haigh: ‘We’re absolutely committed to devolving responsibilities where they can be devolved.’ Photograph: Neil Hall/EPA

Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, was speaking before a speech to the CBI conference on Monday morning at which she was to make the case for greater government control of public utilities.

After the Times reported Natural England was in line to be abolished, Haigh was asked on Sky News about the proliferation of quangos. She said: “We’ve had successive governments complain about this, but unfortunately, successive governments have created more of these and pushed more decision-making out of their own departments, so that then when they make decisions they don’t agree with, they turn around and look in horror.

“That’s why we’re absolutely committed to devolving responsibilities where they can be devolved.”

Asked if she was considering getting rid of Natural England, she said: “We’re considering all arm’slength bodies, both devolving, dissolving, and bringing back into departments, because we cannot continue with this situation where politicians look round and can’t take responsibility for the actions that people have elected their government for.”

Asked again about the specific fate of Natural England in a later interview on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, Haigh again did not push back against the idea it was being targeted for abolition along with other arms-length bodies.

after newsletter promotion

She said: “So all the ALBs are in my sight for either devolving responsibilities that can be pushed down to mayors and strategic authorities, whether they can be brought back into departments under the direct power of the secretary of state, or whether they can be dissolved entirely.”

In a section of her speech about utilities, according to extracts released in advance, Haigh was to say she would “put pragmatism and public interest ahead of failed political ideology”, adding: “Public control is not anti-business – it’s about getting the foundations right, so that private enterprise can do what it does best.”

Saying almost no other nation had so many essential services run by private companies, and often overseas ones at that, Haigh was to say: “The status quo is not the neutral, pragmatic centre ground. It’s the outlier. An exception that no other nation is trying to emulate.”

items.title: Twenty Gaza students due to leave for Ireland after winning visa battle
items.summary: Group’s evacuation follows campaign to overturn decision to deny visas to more than 60 students from territory Twenty students from Gaza are to travel to Ireland to take up scholarships after winning a battle for visas that undercut the Irish government’s reputation as a champion of Palestinians . T…
items.body:
Decision to deny visas dismayed opposition politicians and other critics who accused government of betraying Ireland’s record of solidarity with Palestinians. Photograph: Emilija Jefremova/Reuters

Decision to deny visas dismayed opposition politicians and other critics who accused government of betraying Ireland’s record of solidarity with Palestinians. Photograph: Emilija Jefremova/Reuters

Students from Gaza win visa battle to study in Ireland

Decision to deny visas to more than 60 students overturned after high court orders justice department to reconsider

Twenty students from Gaza are to travel to Ireland to take up scholarships after winning a battle for visas that undercut the Irish government’s reputation as a champion of Palestinians.

The group is due to leave the territory on Monday under strict Israeli controls and travel via Jordan to Dublin to take up places at Irish universities. Another group is expected to follow next month.

The evacuation comes after a four-month campaign to overturn a decision by the Irish Department of Justice to deny visas to more than 60 students in Gaza who had been offered scholarships in Ireland.

The decision dismayed opposition politicians and other critics who accused the department of betraying Ireland’s record of solidarity with Palestinians.

The government backed down last week after a Dublin high court ordered the department to reconsider the decision. The minister for justice, Jim O’Callaghan, approved 48 visas. The first group is expected to arrive on Tuesday, with the remainder coming in late December.

“It’s a mix of feelings I still can’t fully describe,” Amir Alareer, 26, who is to study cybersecurity and artificial intelligence at University College Dublin, said via email on the eve of his departure from Gaza.

“There is hope and relief after months of waiting and fighting for this moment. But it is hard to feel complete joy when I am leaving my family behind in Gaza, and when 28 of my fellow students, who hold the same visas and share the same dreams, are still here waiting.”

The students originally expected to come in summer, and had supporting paperwork from Irish universities, but in July the Department of Justice rejected the visa applications. “The refusals hit us hard,” said Alareer.

The department demanded bank statements, proof of intention to return and other documents and said any appeal would have to be made by post, saying screening and verification were integral to the immigration system.

The students said such documents had not previously been requested and that Gaza’s banking and postal service had been destroyed. Ivana Bacik, a legislator and leader of the Labour party, accused the department of using “spurious reasons” amid a hardening of immigration policy.

Alareer helped to lead a campaign from Gaza that was backed in Ireland by demonstrators, a petition and an open letter signed by actors, writers and artists including Hozier, Nicola Coughlan and the rap group Kneecap. “Running a campaign from Gaza, through blackouts and displacement, was not easy, but I knew that if we stayed silent, our case would be forgotten,” said Alareer.

In October, the high court ruled that there were “significant and demonstrable errors” in the refusal of a visa to Shaymaa Abudalu, a 20-year-old who had been offered an engineering scholarship at University College Cork, and who was the lead case in a batch of similar lawsuits. A high court judge welcomed the decision last week to grant 48 visas and said “huge progress” had been made.

Among the students are five members of a dance troupe who have been offered places at the Irish World Academy of Music and Dance at the University of Limerick.

Alareer, who studied engineering at Al-Azhar University – Gaza, said Israel’s attacks on Gaza had destroyed his home and displaced the family several times. “The hardest experience of all was the famine, when we couldn’t find even a single kilo of flour.” Floods have impeded recent relief efforts.

His family was proud of his scholarship, he said, but saying goodbye would be hard. “They are happy that I finally have this opportunity, but leaving them behind after everything we have been through together is incredibly difficult.”

After studying software and innovation in Dublin, Alareer plans to return to Al-Azhar University and establish a cybersecurity department. “I want to build a generation of Palestinian engineers and researchers who can protect our digital future. Gaza will be rebuilt, and its systems must be rebuilt securely, by its own people.”

items.title: Democrats win largest House majority since 1992 after flipping North Carolina seat
items.summary: Democrats have now won at least 258 seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats.
items.body:
Image source, Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images

Image caption,

Chuck Hubbard is a former journalist whose first political campaign was in 2022

ByMadeline Halpert

The Democratic Party has won the largest majority in the US House of Representatives since 1992, after Democrat Chuck Hubbard unseated Republican Representative Virginia Foxx in North Carolina.

The race was called on Sunday, with Hubbard beating Foxx by 330 votes with 99% counted. It was one of the closest contests of the recent midterm elections, in which Democrats also secured the Senate.

The party has now won at least 258 House seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats, with four races still yet to be called.

Neither party had won as many House races since 1992, when Bill Clinton won the presidency and Democrats won a total of 258 seats.

• View the 2026 midterm election results

Sunday's result came after Foxx, who has represented North Carolina's 5th Congressional District since 2005, requested a recount. This is allowed under state law when the margin of victory is under 1%.

She conceded on Sunday, saying in a statement: "After running a campaign focused on my track record of commonsense solutions and conservative values, I'm humbled and grateful that so many North Carolina voters responded by supporting my candidacy, even if we came up just a few votes short."

Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images

Image caption,

Virginia Foxx spent a decade in the North Carolina Senate before representing the state in the House of Representatives

Hubbard, meanwhile, wrote on X that he had spoken to Foxx, "who graciously conceded following the results of the recount process".

He added: "I deeply appreciate her commitment to a smooth transition of the office and constituent casework. We may not always agree, but we both love North Carolina and the people of the Fifth District."

Hubbard's win, which comes after he lost to Foxx in the 2024 midterms by nine percentage points, followed a number of Democratic victories in deeply Republican districts including South Carolina, Texas, Alaska and Iowa.

Hubbard, like many Democrats running in the midterms, focused on the rising cost of living in the US during the war with Iran - a top issue for voters.

President Donald Trump himself has suggested inflation caused by the war in Iran was probably to blame for the Republican losses, as well as Vice President JD Vance.

Hubbard has also said he will also prioritise working families and small businesses, supporting public education and expanding access to affordable healthcare, according to his website.

The remaining House races yet to be called are in Tennessee and Minnesota, while two elections in Louisiana will go to a runoff in December. In Tennessee's fourth district, Democrat Victoria Broderick leads by fewer than 300 votes, and in Minnesota's first district, Democrat Jake Johnson is winning by fewer than 500 votes.

Democrats may use their upcoming majority in the House and control of the Senate to investigate conflicts of interest and other actions by the president and those close to him, while the Senate also has the power to confirm or block the president's cabinet and judicial nominations. They will also be able to pass legislation through Congress easily, though Trump still has to give final sign off for it to become law.

However, even with control of both chambers of Congress, they will still have limits on their power as Trump can veto legislation.

items.summary: Tata-owned Agratas plant to build EV batteries for sister company Jaguar Land Rover seen as crucial for long-term health of British car industry One of the UK’s flagship electric vehicle battery projects has been thrown into turmoil after its second building contractor in five months walked away, ad…
items.body:
The Freelander 8, the first Freelander-branded electric vehicle jointly developed by British carmaker Jaguar Land Rover and Chinese joint-venture partner Chery displayed at a launch event in Wuhu, China. Photograph: Nick Carey/Reuters

The Freelander 8, the first Freelander-branded electric vehicle jointly developed by British carmaker Jaguar Land Rover and Chinese joint-venture partner Chery displayed at a launch event in Wuhu, China. Photograph: Nick Carey/Reuters

Flagship UK gigafactory plan in turmoil after it loses second builder in five months

Tata-owned Agratas plant to build EV batteries for sister company Jaguar Land Rover seen as crucial for long-term health of British car industry

One of the UK’s flagship electric vehicle battery projects has been thrown into turmoil after its second building contractor in five months walked away, adding to questions over when Jaguar Land Rover cars will use British-made batteries.

The £5.2bn gigafactory in Bridgwater, Somerset, is being built by Agratas, to provide batteries for Britain’s largest automotive employer, its sister company. Agratas and Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) are both part of Indian conglomerate Tata Group.

The UK government has pledged £380m in financial support for the factory because it is seen as crucial to the long-term survival of the British car industry, but the build has suffered several setbacks. The construction specialist contracted by Agratas, TSL, has decided to leave the project after failing to agree terms with Agratas, according to three sources.

Batteries are among the important parts of EVs, but global supply is now dominated by China, South Korea and Japan. Successive Conservative and Labour governments have strongly supported efforts to build a British battery supply chain, and it also fits with Andy Burnham’s hopes to “reindustrialise” the UK. Not all of the subsidy has yet been paid out.

Tata announced the gigafactory in 2023, aiming for a 2026 start of production with as many as 4,200 employees, before pushing it back to 2027. Replacing the lead contractor for the second time in five months is likely to add to doubts over whether Agratas can hit its latest target of January 2028 – although the company has not yet pushed back its planned start date.

A spokesperson for Agratas said: “We are on track to meet our customer requirements.

“The Somerset site is a large and complex industrialisation project, and all of our supplier partners are supporting us well as we prepare for the facility’s launch phase.”

The inability to reach an agreement with TSL, formally known as Tonroe Group, stemmed from disagreements over the timeline and cost of the project, two sources said.

TSL is expected to leave the site within two or three months, leaving no other main build contractor lined up. However, it is thought that NG Bailey, the project’s mechanical, electrical and plumbing contractor, could be one option to take over the entire build.

The issues at the heart of the dispute are similar to those with TSL’s predecessor, Sir Robert McAlpine (SRM). Agratas fired SRM at short notice in June, and one source suggested discussions over the terms of its departure remain ongoing.

Morale within Agratas has also been hit by the company’s decision to relocate some workers from Coventry, in a building shared with other Tata Group companies, to Somerset.

Some of those workers are expected to take redundancy rather than uproot families and move 120 miles away. If they did so it would continue a stream of senior staff leaving the business in recent months, two sources said.

The UK’s only operating gigafactory, AESC’s plant in Sunderland, north-east England, has also faced problems as carmakers have scaled back plans for EVs, with governments delaying bans on petrol and diesel cars. The Guardian revealed in August that AESC had shelved expansion plans after it failed to agree a separate deal to supply JLR.

skip past newsletter promotion

after newsletter promotion

It is understood that JLR has secured batteries from other suppliers, so its plans to increase sales of new electric Land Rovers and Jaguars will not be affected. However, those initial cars will not have British-made batteries, although the manufacturer could also avoid EU tariffs under “rules of origin” if it uses batteries made in Europe.

Agratas has made some progress at the Somerset factory, as well as another site in Sanand, western India. Some Agratas managers have travelled to India this week to share experiences with their counterparts in India and discuss the UK situation.

The shell of the building site in south west England is mostly complete, and National Grid has started work on the electricity substation that will provide the large amounts of power needed to make batteries.

People close to the project suggest Agratas could still succeed in producing batteries and avoid the fate of an earlier rival project, Britishvolt, which collapsed after failing to secure firm orders. The former Britishvolt site in north-east England is now being turned into a datacentre for artificial intelligence – a potentially attractive prospect for an empty building with a high-capacity connection to the electricity grid.

Agratas was approached for comment. TSL declined to comment. JLR declined to comment. NG Bailey was approached for comment.

items.summary: After a warmer-than-average November so far globally, a cold snap is on the horizon in parts of Europe While average global temperatures continue to set records through one of the strongest El Niños on record, temperatures across a large swathe of Europe could plunge this week, as Arctic air sweeps…
items.body:
People on the Charles Bridge in Prague, Czechia, in 2022. As low pressure pushes into western and central Europe, significant snow is expected this week. Photograph: Petr David Josek/AP

People on the Charles Bridge in Prague, Czechia, in 2022. As low pressure pushes into western and central Europe, significant snow is expected this week. Photograph: Petr David Josek/AP

Arctic air brings colder temperatures to Europe this week

After a warmer-than-average November so far globally, a cold snap is on the horizon in parts of Europe

While average global temperatures continue to set records through one of the strongest El Niños on record, temperatures across a large swathe of Europe could plunge this week, as Arctic air sweeps in.

On Friday, the global average temperature was 2.12C higher than the preindustrial average, the biggest ever anomaly and equivalent to 1.22C above the 1991-2020 climate average.

But in parts of Europe, high pressure building over Scandinavia and low pressure shifting south-east into western Russia will open a corridor of cold air from the north. Temperatures in the Baltics and in countries such as Germany, Poland and Ukraine are likely to fall widely below zero from Monday, with ice days – in which temperatures stay below 0C all day – expected from midweek. By the weekend, temperatures could be 5-15C below average, reaching double-digit negatives on higher ground.

The low pressure over eastern Europe and western Russia will bring extensive snowfall. Southern Poland, Belarus, eastern Ukraine and south-eastern parts of the Baltics will be the first to see widespread snow, which could reach up to 10cm in southern Poland.

Temperatures are expected to fall below zero in Germany, Austria and Czechia. Photograph: Peeradon Warithkorasuth/Getty Images

Later in the week, as a smaller area of low pressure pushes into western and central Europe, significant snow is expected to spread across southern Germany, Austria and Czechia, where depths of 10-20cm could build. The Alps could get a significant dumping of snow, a welcome boost for the region’s ski resorts which will open in the coming weeks.

Into the weekend and the start of December, high pressure is set to remain dominant across northern Europe, maintaining below-average temperatures in central and eastern Europe and possibly extending into the Balkans. There are also hints that the sudden stratospheric warming earlier this month could finally begin influencing the lower atmosphere, with high pressure extending farther west and perhaps bringing cold easterly winds into western Europe and the UK, although confidence on this is low.

The cold in Europe is in stark contrast to the global picture. This October was the warmest on record, with an average global temperature of 15.35C, 0.9C above the 1991-2020 average and 1.75C above the estimated preindustrial level. It was the third month in a row above 1.5C, following August and September, and while parts of Europe, including the UK, have seen below-average temperatures so far this November, global temperatures this month have continued to run above average.
